why_how.text: Speed turns minor mishaps into fatal ones, so the speed laws protect everyone on the road.
Knowing the statutory limits tells you the top speed where no other zone is posted.

scenario.text: Lee drives on a county paved road with no speed sign posted.

reasoning.text: Statutory limits apply unless another zone is posted, and the county paved road limit is forty-five miles per hour unless posted.

result.text: Lee keeps to forty-five or less, slower if conditions make that unreasonable.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking driving at the posted limit is always lawful.

correction.text: The basic speed law says never drive faster than is reasonable for road, weather, vehicle and personal conditions.

memory_support.text: Thirty town, thirty-five dirt, forty-five county, fifty-five elsewhere.

prompt.text: With no zone posted, what is the statutory limit in an urban district?

rationale.text: Statutory limits are thirty in an urban district, thirty-five on an unpaved road and forty-five on a county paved road unless posted.

narration.text: Traffic laws cover everyone on the road: drivers, motorcycle and bicycle riders, and pedestrians. The Legislature changes traffic laws from time to time, so every driver should restudy the manual every few years. This lesson begins the chapter with speed. Speed often turns a minor mishap into a fatal one, and its main danger is making collisions more severe rather than more frequent. You will learn the basic speed law, what exceeding a limit means, the statutory limits on different roads, minimum speeds, and the places where you must slow down.

lines.text: Over the limit is evidence of unlawful speed.

narration.text: Alabama's basic speed law says never drive faster than is reasonable for current road, weather, vehicle and personal conditions. On top of that, going faster than a speed limit is prima facie evidence of unlawful speed and can get you arrested, and every limit inside a municipality is a maximum. Statutory limits apply unless a different speed zone has been set and posted on official regulatory signs. So the posted or statutory number is the top of the range, and the basic speed law can require you to go slower than that number when conditions call for it.

lines.text: Thirty urban, thirty-five unpaved, forty-five county.
Fifty-five elsewhere; sixty-five, seventy where posted.

narration.text: Statutory limits are thirty miles per hour in an urban district, thirty-five on an unpaved road, and forty-five on a county paved road unless posted. Elsewhere the statutory limit is fifty-five miles per hour, with sixty-five where posted and seventy where posted on an interstate. These limits apply wherever a different speed zone has not been set and posted. So if you see no sign, think about the kind of road you are on: town street, unpaved road, county paved road, or another road, and use the statutory limit that matches it. Never drive faster than is reasonable for conditions.

lines.text: Slow at crossings, crests and curves.

narration.text: Where a minimum speed is posted, going slower is unlawful in normal conditions, and you must never drive so slowly that you hold up traffic. Speed also has to drop in certain places. Slow down near street, highway and railroad crossings, near flags, flares or fuses on the road, and when approaching hill crests and curves. These are the places where hazards appear suddenly or where you cannot see far ahead, so a lower speed gives you time to react. Driving too slowly and driving too fast can both be problems. Never drive faster than is reasonable for conditions.

title.text: The limit is not a promise

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think any speed up to the limit is lawful. But Alabama's basic speed law says never drive faster than is reasonable for current road, weather, vehicle and personal conditions. On a wet, foggy night, the posted or statutory limit may be far too fast. Going over a limit is prima facie evidence of unlawful speed, but going under it does not guarantee you are lawful. So when a question describes poor conditions, the safe and legal answer is a speed reasonable for those conditions, which may be well below the limit.

lines.text: No sign in a town: what limit?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: with no zone posted, what is the statutory limit in an urban district? Decide on your answer first. The answer is thirty miles per hour. Statutory limits are thirty in an urban district, thirty-five on an unpaved road and forty-five on a county paved road unless posted, with fifty-five elsewhere, sixty-five where posted and seventy where posted on an interstate. These statutory limits apply unless a different speed zone has been set and posted on regulatory signs, and the basic speed law can require you to go slower.

To close, traffic laws cover every road user, and because they change you should restudy the manual every few years. Speed mainly makes crashes more severe. Never drive faster than is reasonable for conditions, and remember that exceeding a limit is prima facie evidence of unlawful speed, with every municipal limit a maximum. Statutory limits apply unless another zone is posted: thirty urban, thirty-five unpaved, forty-five county paved, and fifty-five elsewhere, with sixty-five or seventy where posted. A posted minimum makes slower driving unlawful in normal conditions, and you slow down near crossings, flares, crests and curves.

why_how.text: Knowing exactly where and when to stop prevents crashes at intersections and crossings.

scenario.text: Kim reaches an intersection where the traffic light is completely dark.

reasoning.text: The manual says to treat an intersection with a dead traffic light as a four-way stop.

result.text: Kim comes to a full stop and takes her turn as she would at a four-way stop.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may turn left on red from any street once you have stopped.

correction.text: A left turn on red after stopping is allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street whose traffic moves right to left.

memory_support.text: Flashing red means STOP; dark light means four-way stop.

prompt.text: What should you do at an intersection where the signal lights are out?

answer.text: Treat it as a four-way stop.

rationale.text: The manual says to treat an intersection with a dead traffic light as a four-way stop.

narration.text: This lesson lists the places and situations where you must come to a complete stop. You will learn exactly where to stop at a STOP sign, when a second stop is needed, where to stop when leaving an alley or driveway, and when to stop for a school patrol. Then you will see the rules for red lights, including the limited cases when you may turn on red, what to do when a light is dark or flashing red, and the other places where you must stop, including for emergency vehicles. These stops are some of the most common test topics. A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign.

lines.text: Stop at the line, crosswalk or view point.
Stop before the sidewalk leaving driveways.

narration.text: At a STOP sign, stop at the marked line; with no line, before the near crosswalk; with neither, at the point nearest the cross street where you can see traffic. A second stop may be needed when something blocked your view at the first one and cross traffic is coming. Coming out of an alley, private driveway or building in a business or residence district, always stop before the sidewalk or crosswalk area. And you must stop when a school patrol member holds an official flag in the STOP position. Each of these protects people who may be crossing in front of you.

lines.text: Left on red only one-way to one-way.

narration.text: At a red light, wait for green and a clear way, though you may turn right after stopping if you are in the proper lane. A left turn on red after stopping is allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street whose traffic moves right to left. Any turn on red must yield to traffic and pedestrians lawfully in the intersection and is not allowed where a sign prohibits it. Treat an intersection with a dead traffic light as a four-way stop, and remember that a flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign. A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign.

lines.text: Emergency vehicles: pull over and stop.

narration.text: You must also stop at railroad crossings posted with STOP signs or when a flagman or device there directs, at bridges opening for boats, and when a construction flagman or police officer orders it. For an emergency vehicle with flashing red or blue lights and a siren, whether ahead or behind, pull to the curb or roadside and stop completely. In each case someone or something is directing traffic for safety, and your job is to stop and wait until it is safe or until you are told to go. These stops are required by law, not left to your judgment.

lines.text: Traffic must move right to left.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because a right turn on red after stopping is common, some drivers assume a left on red works the same way. It does not. A left turn on red after stopping is allowed only from a one-way street onto a one-way street whose traffic moves right to left. And any turn on red, right or left, must yield to traffic and pedestrians lawfully in the intersection and is not allowed where a sign prohibits it. So on an ordinary two-way street, a left turn on red is not allowed, even after a full stop. A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign.

lines.text: Signal lights are out: what now?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what should you do at an intersection where the signal lights are out? Decide on your answer first. The answer is to treat it as a four-way stop. Come to a complete stop and take your turn in order. Do not confuse this with a flashing red signal, which means the same as a STOP sign, or with a red light, where you wait for green unless you may turn right, or in the one-way case left, after stopping. A dark light gives no right of way to anyone, so everyone stops. A flashing red signal means the same as a STOP sign. Every turn on red must yield.

lines.text: STOP signs, reds, darks, flashing red.

narration.text: To sum up, at a STOP sign stop at the line, before the near crosswalk, or where you can see the cross street, and stop again if your view was blocked. Stop before the sidewalk when leaving an alley or driveway, and for a school patrol's STOP flag. At a red light you may turn right after stopping, but left only from one one-way street onto another moving right to left, and every turn on red yields. A dead light is a four-way stop, a flashing red is a STOP sign, and you stop for railroad STOP signs, flaggers, opening bridges, officers and emergency vehicles.

why_how.text: School bus rules protect children getting on and off, amber lights warn of a stop, and drivers from both directions often must stop.

scenario.text: Pat is driving on a divided highway of four lanes, and a school bus is stopped with its arm out in the opposing roadway.

reasoning.text: No stop is needed on a divided highway of four or more lanes when the bus is in the opposing roadway.

result.text: Pat continues carefully, but would have to stop if the highway were undivided.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you never need to stop for a bus on the other side of a four-lane road.

correction.text: On a four to six lane undivided highway you must stop; the exception applies only to divided highways of four or more lanes.

memory_support.text: Amber get ready, red stop twenty feet back.

prompt.text: A bus's amber lights start flashing ahead of you. What do they signal?

answer.text: That the bus is about to stop to load or unload children.

rationale.text: Flashing amber lights are a pre-warning that the bus is preparing to stop.

lines.text: When to stop for a bus.

narration.text: School buses and church buses stop often to let passengers on and off, and the law requires other drivers to stop too. In this lesson you will learn when you must stop for a stopped school or church bus, how that rule applies on undivided highways, the one exception for divided highways and loading zones, and what the amber and red lights on a school bus mean. You will also learn how far ahead the amber lights come on and how far back you must stop. These rules protect children at their most vulnerable moments. On an undivided highway, traffic from both directions stops.

lines.text: Arm out and red lights: stop.
Undivided four to six lanes too.

narration.text: Following or meeting a stopped school or church bus with its stop arm out and red lights flashing, stop and stay stopped until the arm folds and the lights go off. That stop also applies on a four to six lane undivided highway. No stop is needed on a divided highway of four or more lanes when the bus is in the opposing roadway, or when the bus is in a roadside loading zone where pedestrians may not cross. So on an undivided road, traffic from both directions stops, and the exception depends on a divided highway or a protected loading zone.

lines.text: Red and arm: stop twenty feet back.

narration.text: Flashing amber lights on a school bus are a pre-warning that it is about to stop to load or unload children. The amber lights come on at least three hundred feet before the stop in rural areas and at least one hundred feet before it in municipalities. Red flashing lights with the stop arm out mean the bus is loading or unloading, and drivers from either direction stop at least twenty feet from it. So amber bus lights mean get ready, while red lights and the stop arm mean stop at least twenty feet away. On an undivided highway, traffic from both directions stops.

lines.text: Divided four-plus lanes: opposite side may go.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers believe they never need to stop for a bus on the far side of a four-lane road. The manual says the stop applies on a four to six lane undivided highway. Only on a divided highway of four or more lanes, when the bus is in the opposing roadway, or when the bus is in a roadside loading zone where pedestrians may not cross, is no stop needed. So the key word is divided. Without a divider separating you from the bus, you stop and stay stopped until the arm folds and the lights go off. On an undivided highway, traffic from both directions stops.

lines.text: Amber lights flash: what do they signal?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: a bus's amber lights start flashing ahead of you. What do they signal? Decide first, then listen. The answer is that the bus is about to stop to load or unload children. Amber lights are a pre-warning that come on at least three hundred feet before the stop in rural areas and at least one hundred feet in municipalities. When the red lights flash and the stop arm comes out, you must stop at least twenty feet from the bus and stay stopped until the arm folds and the lights go off. On an undivided highway, traffic from both directions stops.

lines.text: Arm out: stop, both ways if undivided.

narration.text: To wrap up, when a school or church bus is stopped with its arm out and red lights flashing, stop and stay stopped until the arm folds and the lights go off, whether you are following or meeting it, including on four to six lane undivided highways. No stop is needed on a divided highway of four or more lanes when the bus is in the opposing roadway, or at a roadside loading zone where pedestrians may not cross. Amber lights warn of a coming stop, at least three hundred feet ahead in rural areas and one hundred in towns, and with red lights you stop at least twenty feet away.

why_how.text: Breaking right-of-way rules is one of the main causes of crashes, whether at an intersection or pulling out of a driveway.
Yielding rules tell you who goes first when paths cross.

scenario.text: Two cars reach an uncontrolled intersection from different roads at about the same time; Sam is on the left.

reasoning.text: The vehicle on the left yields to the vehicle on the right.

result.text: Sam yields and lets the car on the right go first.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a green arrow means you never have to yield.

correction.text: Drivers entering on a green arrow still yield to traffic lawfully using the intersection.

memory_support.text: Left yields right; driveway yields road.

prompt.text: You are pulling out of a private driveway onto a busy street. What must you do?

answer.text: Stop and yield to traffic on the public road.

rationale.text: A car coming from a private road or driveway must stop and yield to traffic on the public road.

narration.text: Breaking right-of-way rules is one of the main causes of crashes, and the rules rest on courtesy and common sense. In this lesson you will learn who yields at an uncontrolled intersection, how speed can cost you the right of way, what to do for emergency vehicles, the duty to stop for blind pedestrians, the rules for driveways and YIELD signs, and how left turns and green arrows work. Each rule answers the same question, who goes first when two paths cross, and knowing the answers makes your driving predictable to others. At an uncontrolled intersection the left yields to the right.

lines.text: Unlawful speed loses right of way.

narration.text: When two vehicles from different roads reach an uncontrolled intersection at about the same time, the one on the left yields to the one on the right. Entering an uncontrolled intersection at an unlawful speed forfeits any right of way you would have had. So the rule protects drivers who approach at a lawful speed, and a driver who speeds into the intersection cannot claim the right of way even if they would otherwise have had it. At any uncontrolled intersection, slow down enough to be able to yield if a vehicle is approaching on your right.

lines.text: Pull over and stop for emergencies.
Stop for a cane or guide dog.

narration.text: For an emergency vehicle, pull over and stop whether it is overtaking or meeting you, but clear an intersection first, and wait until it passes. At any intersection you must stop for a blind person using a guide dog or holding out a red-tipped white cane. These are two cases where you give way completely: the emergency vehicle needs a clear path, and a blind pedestrian cannot see your car. Clearing the intersection before stopping matters, because stopping in the middle of it could block the emergency vehicle's path. At an uncontrolled intersection the left yields to the right.

A car coming from a private road or driveway must stop and yield to traffic on the public road. At a YIELD sign facing you, slow down and stop if needed for vehicles and pedestrians lawfully crossing. Turning left, yield to oncoming vehicles in the intersection or close enough to be an immediate hazard. Drivers entering on a green arrow still yield to traffic lawfully using the intersection. In each case, the driver making the riskier move, entering a road or turning across traffic, is the one who waits for a safe moment. At an uncontrolled intersection the left yields to the right.

Here is the trap. A green arrow feels like total permission, but drivers entering on a green arrow still yield to traffic lawfully using the intersection. The same idea applies to a YIELD sign, where you slow and stop if needed, and to left turns, where you yield to oncoming vehicles that are close enough to be an immediate hazard. So no signal or sign removes your duty to avoid hitting someone who is already lawfully in the intersection. Look before you go, even when the arrow is green. At an uncontrolled intersection the left yields to the right.

Here is a quick check: you are pulling out of a private driveway onto a busy street. What must you do? Decide on your answer first. The answer is to stop and yield to traffic on the public road. A car coming from a private road or driveway must stop and yield. Remember too that leaving an alley or driveway in a business or residence district means stopping before the sidewalk or crosswalk area, so you may stop once for pedestrians and again for traffic before you enter the street. At an uncontrolled intersection the left yields to the right.

lines.text: Left yields right; speeders lose it.
Yield to emergencies, blind walkers, oncoming.

narration.text: To close, right-of-way violations are one of the main causes of crashes. At an uncontrolled intersection, the vehicle on the left yields to the one on the right, and entering at an unlawful speed forfeits your right of way. For an emergency vehicle, clear the intersection and pull over and stop until it passes. Stop for a blind person with a guide dog or red-tipped white cane. Driveway traffic stops and yields, a YIELD sign means slow and stop if needed, left turns yield to oncoming traffic, and green-arrow drivers still yield to those lawfully inside.

why_how.text: Careless passing causes many head-on and sideswipe crashes on two-lane highways, so both the passing driver and the driver being passed have duties.

scenario.text: Jordan is on a two-lane road approaching a hill and wants to pass a slow truck.

reasoning.text: You may not cross the center line to pass on a curve or hill unless you can see a clear passing distance of at least five hundred feet.

result.text: Jordan stays behind the truck until the road ahead is clear for five hundred feet or more.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking you may use the shoulder to pass a slow car on the right.

correction.text: Using the shoulder to pass is unlawful except in an emergency or when traffic authorities direct it.

memory_support.text: Clear, legal, signaled, and back with room.

prompt.text: Another driver begins passing you on a two-lane road. What should you do?

answer.text: Keep to your lane and do not speed up.

rationale.text: When someone is passing you, stay in your lane and do not increase your speed.

narration.text: Head-on and sideswipe crashes on two-lane highways, mostly from careless passing, cause many deaths and serious injuries. Beyond the marked no-passing areas, you must use extreme care everywhere in darkness, poor visibility, and on roads slick from rain, snow or ice. In this lesson you will learn when you may pass on the left, how to check, signal and return, what to do when you are being passed, when passing on the right is allowed, why the shoulder is off limits, and the places where you may not cross the center line to pass. Pass only where you can finish within the speed limit.

On a two-way, two-lane road you may pass on the left only if you can finish safely without exceeding the speed limit. Before passing, check far enough ahead and behind for drivers about to pass you, and alert the driver ahead with a horn tap, or a headlight flick at night. Signal left before passing and right before moving back, returning only when the passed car's whole front shows in your inside mirror. When someone is passing you, keep to your lane and do not speed up. Every step here is about leaving enough room and making your plan clear.

Passing on the right is allowed on one-way roads and on roads marked for two or more lanes going the same way. Using the shoulder to pass is unlawful except in an emergency or when traffic authorities direct it. A signal alone gives no right to pass on the right; check both ways and watch the car closely, since some states forbid the move and drivers from there may not expect it. So passing on the right is a legal but careful move on the right kind of road, and never a reason to drive onto the shoulder. Pass only where you can finish within the speed limit.

lines.text: Curves and hills: five hundred feet clear.
Intersections, oncoming cars, signs, solid line.

narration.text: Do not cross the center line to pass on a curve or hill unless you can see a clear passing distance of at least five hundred feet. Do not cross it to pass at a highway intersection, when meeting oncoming traffic, where signs forbid it, or with a solid yellow line on your side, and remember that double solid yellow bars both directions. Each of these places either hides oncoming traffic or puts other vehicles where you would be moving. When any of them applies, stay in your lane and wait for a safer place. Pass only where you can finish within the speed limit.

title.text: The shoulder is not a lane

narration.text: Here is the trap. When a car ahead slows to turn left, it can be tempting to slip past it on the right using the shoulder. That is unlawful except in an emergency or when traffic authorities direct it. Passing on the right is only allowed on one-way roads and on roads marked for two or more lanes going the same way, and even then a signal alone does not give you the right to pass. So if the only way past is the shoulder, wait. The shoulder is for emergencies, not for getting around slow traffic. Pass only where you can finish within the speed limit.

lines.text: Someone is passing you: what to do?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: another driver begins passing you on a two-lane road. What should you do? Decide on your answer first. The answer is to keep to your lane and not speed up. Holding your speed steady, or easing off if the pass looks tight, helps the other driver get back in safely. Speeding up would trap them in the oncoming lane. When you are the one passing, remember to signal left before passing and right before moving back, and to return only when the passed car's whole front shows in your inside mirror. Pass only where you can finish within the speed limit.

lines.text: Pass left only within the limit.
No shoulder; no blind curves or hills.

narration.text: To finish, careless passing causes many deaths on two-lane highways, so use extreme care in darkness, poor visibility and on slick roads. Pass on the left only if you can finish without exceeding the limit, after checking ahead and behind and alerting the driver. Signal left, then right, and return when the whole front of the passed car shows in your mirror. When being passed, keep your lane and do not speed up. Pass on the right only on one-way or multi-lane roads, never on the shoulder, and never cross the center line on curves or hills without five hundred feet of view, at intersections, with oncoming traffic, where signs forbid it, or with a solid yellow line on your side.

why_how.text: Pedestrian injuries could be greatly reduced if drivers were more observant, and walkers can help by walking left and staying visible.

scenario.text: Riley is waiting at a red light, and the car's front end is creeping into the crosswalk.

reasoning.text: Drivers must keep crosswalks clear while waiting at a stop sign or red light.

result.text: Riley stops behind the crosswalk so pedestrians can cross safely.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking drivers must always yield to pedestrians wherever they cross.

correction.text: Pedestrians crossing anywhere other than a crosswalk must yield to all vehicles.

memory_support.text: Watch where people gather; give hoses and sirens room.

prompt.text: A friend is walking along a road at night with no sidewalk. How should they walk?

answer.text: Far left in single file, with a light or light or reflective clothing.

rationale.text: Walkers on a roadway keep far left in single file, carry a light or wear light or reflective clothing at night, and make eye contact with drivers.

narration.text: This lesson covers your duties to people on foot and two rules about emergency vehicles. You will learn where to watch hardest for pedestrians, the things drivers must do for school children, safety patrols, blind walkers and buses, the duty pedestrians have when crossing outside a crosswalk, and how people should walk on a roadway. Then you will see how close you may follow an emergency vehicle on a run and the rule about fire hoses. Paying close attention to people on foot can prevent many of the most tragic crashes. Watch hardest where people gather.

Watch hardest for pedestrians near parked cars, in darkness, near schools and play areas, and near churches, mailboxes and bus stops. These are the places where people step out unexpectedly or are hard to see. Drivers must stop for school children and safety patrols, yield to blind walkers, keep crosswalks clear while waiting at a stop sign or light, and stop for a bus with its stop arm out. So in these high-risk places, slow down, scan both sides of the road, and be ready to stop for someone who appears from between parked cars. Watch hardest where people gather.

lines.text: Walk left, single file, be visible.

narration.text: Pedestrians have duties too. Pedestrians crossing anywhere other than a crosswalk must yield to all vehicles. Walkers on a roadway keep far left in single file, carry a light or wear light or reflective clothing at night, and make eye contact with drivers. Walking on the left means facing oncoming traffic, so walkers can see cars coming. For drivers, these rules explain why you will often see pedestrians on the left side of a rural road at night, and why you should still be ready to stop even when the walker is the one who should yield. Watch hardest where people gather.

lines.text: No following within five hundred feet.
Never drive over a fire hose.

narration.text: Only vehicles on necessary official business may follow within five hundred feet of an emergency vehicle on a run. Never drive over an unprotected fire hose unless a police officer or fire official authorizes it. Following an emergency vehicle too closely can put you in the middle of an emergency scene and in the way of other responders. Driving over a hose can damage it and cut off water to firefighters. So when emergency crews are working, keep your distance and wait for an officer or fire official to direct you. Watch hardest where people gather.

lines.text: Drivers still watch and stop if needed.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some learners think drivers must always give way to pedestrians wherever they cross. The manual says pedestrians crossing anywhere other than a crosswalk must yield to all vehicles. That does not mean you may ignore them; drivers still watch hardest near parked cars, schools, play areas and bus stops, and must stop for school children, patrols, blind walkers and buses with their arms out. So a question about a person crossing mid-block, away from a crosswalk, is testing the rule that the pedestrian is the one who must yield.

Here is a quick check: a friend is walking along a road at night with no sidewalk. How should they walk? Decide on your answer first. The answer is far left in single file, carrying a light or wearing light or reflective clothing, and making eye contact with drivers. Walking on the left means facing oncoming traffic. As a driver, remember that pedestrians crossing outside a crosswalk must yield to all vehicles, but you must still watch hardest for people near parked cars, in darkness, and near schools, churches, mailboxes and bus stops. Watch hardest where people gather.

To sum up, watch hardest for pedestrians near parked cars, in darkness, near schools and play areas, and near churches, mailboxes and bus stops. Drivers must stop for school children and safety patrols, yield to blind walkers, keep crosswalks clear while waiting, and stop for a bus with its stop arm out. Pedestrians crossing outside a crosswalk must yield to all vehicles, and walkers on a roadway keep far left in single file, stay visible at night and make eye contact with drivers. Only vehicles on official business may follow within five hundred feet of an emergency vehicle on a run, and never drive over an unprotected fire hose without permission.

why_how.text: Backing, lane changes and turns cause many crashes, so careful looks and clear hand signals matter.
Load rules keep the driver's view clear and protect other road users.

scenario.text: Casey needs to back out of a driveway onto a three-lane street.

reasoning.text: Before backing, walk around the car and look front, sides and rear, then back out only into the nearest lane, never across other lanes.

result.text: Casey checks around the car, backs into the nearest lane and drives forward from there.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking a turn signal gives you the right to change lanes.

correction.text: A signal shows your intention, but before changing lanes you must check clearance beside, ahead and behind and glance at the blind spot.

memory_support.text: Walk around, look back, nearest lane.

prompt.text: What is the hand signal for stopping or slowing down?

rationale.text: Hand signals are arm down to stop or slow, arm straight out for a left turn, and arm up for a right turn.

narration.text: This lesson gathers several everyday traffic laws. You will learn how to back safely and where backing is banned, why driving on the shoulder and blocking your windows are against the law, how to change lanes safely, the hand signals for stopping and turning, why improper turns are so dangerous, and the rules for loads and front-seat passengers. These may seem like small rules, but backing, lane changes and turns are where drivers most often fail to see another vehicle or a person until it is too late. A signal does not give you the right to move.

lines.text: Walk around; look over your right shoulder.

narration.text: Before backing, walk around the car, then look front, sides and rear and keep looking over your right shoulder, not trusting the mirror. Backing is banned on freeways and expressways except for emergency vehicles on duty. Back out of a driveway only into the nearest lane, never across other lanes. Aside from backing into a parking space, backing on a public street or road is never advisable, and drivers should follow the same backing rules when pulling out from angle parking into traffic. Backing is one of the most dangerous moves, so treat it slowly and carefully every time. A signal does not give you the right to move.

lines.text: Check the blind spot before moving.

narration.text: Driving on the shoulder is unlawful except in emergency conditions. State law bars any sign, poster or other material that obstructs a vehicle window. Before changing lanes, check clearance beside, ahead and behind, and glance over your shoulder at the blind spot; a signal does not give you the right to move. Each of these rules keeps you where other drivers expect you to be and lets you see clearly. A clear window, a quick look over the shoulder, and staying off the shoulder all prevent surprises for you and for others. A signal does not give you the right to move.

lines.text: Down: stop. Out: left. Up: right.

narration.text: Hand signals are simple: arm down to stop or slow, arm straight out for a left turn, and arm up for a right turn. Improper turns cause many crashes, and the pedestrian at an intersection is often the one hurt. So signal your turns clearly, by lights or by hand, and make each turn correctly from the proper lane. When you turn at an intersection, look for people in the crosswalk before you complete the turn, because they are the ones most at risk when a driver turns carelessly. A signal does not give you the right to move. Never trust the mirror alone.

lines.text: Five feet beyond front or rear.
Flag by day, light by night.

narration.text: It is unlawful to drive with a load, or more than three people in the front seat, that blocks the driver's view or control. A load may stick out no more than five feet beyond the front and rear of the vehicle. A load reaching four feet or more past the rear needs a red flag at least twelve inches square by day and a red light visible for two hundred feet at night. These rules keep your view clear and make long loads visible to drivers behind you, especially after dark. A signal does not give you the right to move. Never trust the mirror alone.

Here is the trap. Many drivers switch on a signal and move over, as if the signal reserves the space. A signal does not give you the right to change lanes. Before you move, check clearance beside, ahead and behind, and glance over your shoulder at the blind spot your mirror does not cover. The same thinking applies to backing: do not trust the mirror alone, but look over your right shoulder. Signals and mirrors are tools, but your own careful look is what tells you the space is actually clear. A signal does not give you the right to move. Never trust the mirror alone.

lines.text: Hand signal to stop or slow?

narration.text: Here is a quick check: what is the hand signal for stopping or slowing down? Decide on your answer first. The answer is arm extended downward. An arm straight out means a left turn, and an arm up means a right turn. These are the same signals cyclists use. You might use them when your signal lights are hard to see or not working. Whatever signal you use, remember it shows your intention but does not give you the right to move, so check around you before turning or changing lanes. A signal does not give you the right to move. Never trust the mirror alone.

lines.text: Walk around; nearest lane; no freeway backing.

narration.text: To wrap up, before backing walk around the car and look over your right shoulder, never back on freeways or across other lanes, and remember backing on a public street or road is never advisable except into a parking place. Drive on the shoulder only in an emergency, and keep windows free of signs and posters. Before changing lanes, check beside, ahead and behind and glance at the blind spot, because a signal does not give you the right to move. Hand signals are down to stop, out for left and up for right. Improper turns often hurt pedestrians. Loads may extend five feet front and rear, and a load four feet or more past the rear needs a red flag by day and a red light at night.

why_how.text: Knowing what to do at a traffic stop keeps you, your passengers and the officer safe.
Insurance, tint and move-over laws carry fines and protect people working on the road.

scenario.text: Dana is pulled over at night, and her registration is in the glove box.

reasoning.text: At night turn on the interior lights, keep both hands on the wheel, and tell the officer before reaching for papers out of reach.

result.text: Dana turns on the interior light, keeps her hands on the wheel, and tells the officer where the registration is before reaching for it.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking signing a traffic citation means you admit guilt.

correction.text: Signing a citation does not admit guilt, but refusing one may get you arrested; contest it in court instead of arguing.

memory_support.text: Hands on wheel, papers when told, move over for flashers.

prompt.text: You approach a stopped emergency vehicle on a four-lane road. What does the move-over law require?

answer.text: Leave the lane next to the stopped vehicle.

rationale.text: On roads of four or more lanes, leave the lane next to a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights or a wrecker with amber lights.

narration.text: This final lesson of the chapter covers what to do during a law enforcement stop and three laws that every driver must follow. You will learn the steps when you are pulled over, what to tell the officer, how to handle your documents, what signing a citation means, and how to report an officer you think acted wrongly. Then you will see Alabama's mandatory liability insurance law and its minimums and penalties, the window tint limits, and the move-over law for stopped emergency vehicles and wreckers. These rules protect you, officers and road workers.

lines.text: Pull off; engine and radio off.
Hands on the wheel; devices down.

narration.text: When stopped by police, signal and pull off safely, turn off the engine and radio, and stay inside unless told to get out. Keep both hands on the wheel, ask passengers to stay calm with hands visible, put devices down, and turn on interior lights at night. Tell the officer at first contact about any weapons, and do not reach for your license or papers until told to. If your license, insurance proof or registration is out of reach, tell the officer before you reach for it. These steps make your actions clear and predictable to the officer. Keep your hands where the officer can see them.

At a traffic stop you need your driver license, proof of insurance and vehicle registration. An officer out of uniform will show credentials, and you may ask to see them. Signing a citation does not admit guilt, but refusing one may get you arrested; contest it in court instead of arguing at the roadside. If you think an officer acted wrongly, record the time, date, place and details and report it promptly to the officer's agency. So the roadside is the place to cooperate, and the court or the agency is the place to dispute. Keep your hands where the officer can see them.

lines.text: Tint limits on windshield and windows.

narration.text: Alabama's Mandatory Liability Insurance Law bars operating or registering a road vehicle without liability insurance. Minimum coverage is twenty-five thousand dollars for one person's injury or death, fifty thousand for two or more, and twenty-five thousand for property damage. An insurance violation can bring a fine up to five hundred dollars the first time, up to one thousand after that, and or a six month suspension. On every vehicle only the top six inches of the windshield may be tinted. Passenger car side and rear windows need tint passing at least thirty-two percent of light, while SUVs, trucks, vans and RVs follow that only for front side windows and may have darker tint behind the driver.

lines.text: Four-plus lanes: leave the next lane.
Cannot move or two lanes: slow fifteen.

narration.text: On roads of four or more lanes, leave the lane next to a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing lights or a wrecker with amber lights. If you cannot move over, slow to at least fifteen miles per hour under the limit. On two lanes, move away within your lane and slow fifteen under when the limit is twenty-five or more, or go ten where it is twenty or less. So move-over means leave the adjacent lane on four or more lanes, but only slow down when you cannot change lanes or are on two lanes. Keep your hands where the officer can see them. Move over for stopped emergency vehicles and wreckers.

lines.text: Slowing is for when you cannot.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some drivers think the move-over law only asks them to slow down. On roads of four or more lanes, the first duty is to leave the lane next to the stopped emergency vehicle or wrecker. Slowing to at least fifteen miles per hour under the limit is what you do when you cannot move over. On a two-lane road, you move away within your lane and slow fifteen under when the limit is twenty-five or more, or go ten where it is twenty or less. Moving over and slowing are two separate steps for two situations. Keep your hands where the officer can see them.

Here is a quick check: you approach a stopped emergency vehicle on a four-lane road. What does the move-over law require? Decide on your answer first. The answer is to leave the lane next to the stopped vehicle. The same applies to a wrecker displaying amber lights. If you cannot move over safely, slow to at least fifteen miles per hour under the posted limit instead. And on a two-lane road, you move as far away as you can within your own lane and slow down, rather than changing lanes. Keep your hands where the officer can see them. Move over for stopped emergency vehicles and wreckers.

To close the chapter, at a traffic stop pull off safely, turn off the engine and radio, stay inside, keep hands visible, tell the officer about any weapons, and say before reaching for papers out of reach. You need your license, proof of insurance and registration. Signing a citation is not an admission of guilt; contest it in court. Report misconduct to the officer’s agency with details. Carry liability insurance of at least twenty-five, fifty and twenty-five thousand dollars, keep tint within the limits, and on four or more lanes move over for stopped emergency vehicles and wreckers, or slow fifteen under when you cannot.
